author_or_org: Fiona Chen and James Stratton (Harvard University)

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: AI agents produced larger additional increases in code output: 44.0% for lines of code, 36.0% for commits, and 35.7% for pull requests opened.
claims.quote: AI agents lead to larger additional increases in all three measures — 44.0% for lines of code, 36.0% for commits, and 35.7% for pull requests opened.

claims.question: q3
claims.claim: After AI agent adoption, review time from submission to merge rose 56.1%, backlog wait rose 59.9%, active review time rose 58.5%, the share of code changes receiving comments rose 13.1%, and comments per code change rose 38.6%.
claims.quote: after adoption of AI agents, the average time from the code’s review submission to its merge increases by 56.1%. This change represents both an increase in the time that code waits in a “backlog,” by 59.9%, and an increase in the time after code has begun active review, by 58.5%. The latter is consistent with a decline in review productivity, i.e., an increase in the review intensity. The share of code changes that receive at least one review comment increases by 13.1%, and the number of comments on each code change increases by 38.6%.

claims.question: q3
claims.claim: AI code review tools were adopted by 79.1% of firms, but firms still largely kept humans in the loop and humans wrote the overwhelming majority of reviews and comments.
claims.quote: This bottleneck is not eliminated by adoption of AI tools in the review process — 79.1% of firms have adopted AI code review tools, but still largely keep humans in the loop, with the overwhelming majority of reviews and comments being written by humans.

claims.question: q4
claims.claim: Model estimates imply AI agents raised coding productivity by 73.7%, slightly lowered review productivity by −7.0%, reduced coding labor by −22.7%, and increased review labor by 43.4%.
claims.quote: AI agents raise coding productivity by 73.7% and slightly lower review productivity ( −7.0%), and firms shift labor from coding to review: coding labor changes by −22.7% and review labor by 43.4%.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: Qualitative interviews report that outages caused by AI-generated commits led to new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created more review bottlenecks.
claims.quote: After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks.

claims.question: q4
claims.claim: Firm-level employment effects of AI adoption were not statistically significant in noisy estimates: assistants 3.0% with changes below −4.7% ruled out, and agents −2.6% with changes below −15.6% ruled out.
claims.quote: We cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI, though our estimates are noisy. With AI assistants, we estimate an effect of 3.0%, ruling out changes below −4.7%. For AI agents, we estimate an effect of −2.6%, ruling out changes below −15.6%.
